lessons.title: Count Them All
lessons.concept: Joining Two Groups by Counting Every One

play.shortDesc: Touch every object in both groups to find how many there are altogether
play.targetObjective: Count both groups, one object at a time.
stepByStep: Look at the two groups.
Touch every object in the first group, then keep going into the second.
The last number you say is how many there are altogether.
play.kidTip: Do not start again at the second group. Keep counting on.
play.audioPrompt: Count them all! Touch every one in both groups to find how many altogether.

prompts.default: Count them all. How many altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Counting all is where addition starts: a child who counts both groups from one is not behind, they are building the idea the shortcuts will later replace.

lessons.title: Put Them Together

play.shortDesc: Slide two groups into one pile, then count the pile
play.targetObjective: Put the two groups together, then count them.
stepByStep: Look at the two groups on their own.
Tap Put them together to make one pile.
Touch every object in the pile to count it.
play.kidTip: Adding means putting groups together. Then you count once.
play.audioPrompt: Put the two groups together, then count how many you have.

prompts.default: Put the groups together, then count them all.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Seeing two sets physically become one is what makes the plus sign mean something later.

lessons.title: Count On
lessons.concept: Starting from a Number Instead of from One

play.shortDesc: Hold the first number in your head and count on for the rest
play.targetObjective: Say the first number, then count on.
stepByStep: The first group is closed. Its number is written on the lid.
Say that number to yourself — you do not need to count it.
Touch the objects in the second group, counting on from there.
play.kidTip: The closed box is already counted. Start from its number.
play.audioPrompt: Count on! The first group is already counted, so start from its number.

prompts.default: Start at {a} and count on.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Counting on is the first real strategy: it treats the first number as a quantity rather than as something to be re-counted.

lessons.title: Start with the Bigger Number
lessons.concept: Counting On from the Larger Addend

play.shortDesc: Choose the bigger number to start from, so there is less to count
play.targetObjective: Start from the bigger number. It is less work.
stepByStep: Look at both numbers before you start.
Tap the bigger one to start from it.
Count on the smaller group — there are fewer to touch.
play.kidTip: You can add in any order, so start from the bigger number.
play.audioPrompt: Start with the bigger number! Then you have fewer to count on.

prompts.default: Start with the bigger number, then count on.

lessons.pedagogyTip: 3 + 8 and 8 + 3 give the same total, and one of them takes three counts instead of eight. That choice is the lesson.

lessons.title: Adding Zero

play.shortDesc: See that an empty group leaves the total exactly as it was
play.targetObjective: Adding zero leaves the number alone.
stepByStep: One group has objects. The other group is empty.
Nothing is being added, so nothing changes.
Choose the number you started with.
play.kidTip: Zero means none. The number stays the same.
play.audioPrompt: Adding zero! One group is empty, so what happens to the total?

prompts.default: What is {a} plus {b}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Children who have only ever counted find zero genuinely strange — an empty group is still a group, and it still gets added.

lessons.title: Adding One
lessons.concept: One More Is the Next Number

play.shortDesc: Recognise that adding one just moves you to the next counting number
play.targetObjective: One more is the very next number.
stepByStep: Look at how many are in the big group.
One more is being added.
Say the next counting number — that is the answer.
play.kidTip: Adding one is just saying the next number.
play.audioPrompt: Adding one! One more is the next number you say when you count.

prompts.default: What is {a} plus {b}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: This is where the counting sequence stops being a song and starts being arithmetic: the number after seven *is* seven and one more.

lessons.title: Use Your Fingers
lessons.concept: Modelling Both Addends on Two Hands

play.shortDesc: Put one number on each hand, then count all the raised fingers
play.targetObjective: One number on each hand, then count them all.
stepByStep: Raise the first number of fingers on the left hand.
Raise the second number on the right hand.
Count every raised finger to find the total.
play.kidTip: One number on each hand. Then count every finger that is up.
play.audioPrompt: Use your fingers! Put one number on each hand, then count them all.

prompts.default: Show {a} on one hand and {b} on the other. How many fingers altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Fingers are a manipulative a child always has. Discouraging them removes the model before the fact is known, which is what produces guessing.

lessons.title: Five Frame
lessons.concept: Adding Inside a Frame of Five

play.shortDesc: Add counters to a row of five and read the total without counting from one
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame, then read how many.
stepByStep: Some counters are already in the frame.
Tap empty spaces to add the rest.
The frame shows the total — you do not have to start again at one.
play.kidTip: The frame is already counted. Count on from the number in it.
play.audioPrompt: Five frame! Add counters to the row, then say how many there are.

prompts.default: Fill in {b} more. How many are there altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Five is the first benchmark. A child who sees four as 'one less than five' has stopped counting one at a time.

lessons.title: Ten Frame
lessons.concept: Adding Inside a Frame of Ten

play.shortDesc: Add counters to two rows of five and read the total at a glance
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame, then read how many.
stepByStep: The top row holds five. The bottom row holds five more.
Tap empty spaces to add counters.
A full row of five helps you see the total without counting.
play.kidTip: A full top row is five. Count on from there.
play.audioPrompt: Ten frame! Add counters to the frame, then say how many altogether.

prompts.default: Fill in {b} more. How many are there altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Two rows of five is what makes ten readable at a glance, and it is the structure every make-ten strategy later leans on.

lessons.title: Number Bonds

play.shortDesc: Read a bond diagram and give the whole that its two parts make
play.targetObjective: Two parts underneath make the whole on top.
stepByStep: The two boxes at the bottom are the parts.
The box at the top is the whole they make together.
Tap the empty box and type the whole.
play.kidTip: The two parts underneath make the whole on top.
play.audioPrompt: Number bonds! The two parts at the bottom make the whole at the top.

prompts.default: What do {a} and {b} make altogether?

lessons.pedagogyTip: A bond is the picture behind every later decomposition — breaking an addend, finding a missing part, and fact families are all this diagram with a different box blank.

lessons.title: The Number Path

play.shortDesc: Hop forward one square at a time and land on the answer
play.targetObjective: One hop is one number.
stepByStep: The marker starts on the first number.
Each hop moves it forward one square.
Say the number you land on. The last one is the answer.
play.kidTip: One hop is one number. Say each number as you land on it.
play.audioPrompt: The number path! Hop forward one square at a time and see where you land.

prompts.default: Start at {a} and hop forward {b}.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A path has one square per number, so hopping is counting made visible — this is where counting on stops being invisible mental work.

lessons.title: The Open Number Line

play.shortDesc: Take one jump on a line with no numbers, and work out where you landed
play.targetObjective: Nothing on this line tells you where you are.
stepByStep: Only the starting number is marked.
Take the jump — the arc stays on screen.
Work out where you landed and type it in.
play.kidTip: There are no numbers on this line, so keep the count in your head.
play.audioPrompt: The open number line! Take the jump, then work out where you landed.

prompts.default: Start at {a} and jump {b}. Where do you land?

lessons.pedagogyTip: An open line carries no answers, so it stops being a counting aid and becomes a place to record thinking — which is what makes it work for numbers too big to draw.

lessons.title: Base-Ten Blocks
lessons.concept: Adding with Tens and Ones You Can See

play.shortDesc: Build a two-digit answer out of ten-rods and one-units
play.targetObjective: Build the answer out of tens and ones.
stepByStep: Look at the two numbers you are adding.
Tap rods and units in the tray to drop them into the yard.
When the yard holds the answer, check it.
play.kidTip: Build each number out of blocks, then read what you have.
play.audioPrompt: Base-ten blocks! Build the answer out of ten-rods and one-units.

prompts.default: Build {a} plus {b} out of blocks.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A rod is worth ten because it is visibly ten units. A child who can check that is holding place value rather than remembering it.

lessons.title: The Place-Value Chart
lessons.concept: Adding One Column at a Time

play.shortDesc: Write two numbers in tens and ones columns and add each column
play.targetObjective: Ones go under ones. Tens go under tens.
stepByStep: Each number sits in its columns: tens on the left, ones on the right.
Add the ones column, then the tens column.
Write each answer in the column it belongs to.
play.kidTip: Add each column on its own. Ones with ones, tens with tens.
play.audioPrompt: The place-value chart! Add the ones column, then the tens column.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Fill in the total, one column at a time.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Writing the digit in the right column is the skill. A chart that placed it for the child would be teaching something else.

lessons.title: Doubles

play.shortDesc: The Same Number Twice
play.targetObjective: A double is the same number twice.
stepByStep: Read the fact on the card.
Look at the two equal rows.
Type the total and check it.
play.kidTip: A double is the same number twice.
play.audioPrompt: Doubles! The same number twice — these are the facts to know by heart.

prompts.default: Double {a}. What is the total?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Doubles are learned as pictures rather than counted, and they are the anchor every near-double leans on afterwards.

lessons.title: Near Doubles: One More

play.shortDesc: A Double, and One More
play.targetObjective: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
stepByStep: Read the fact on the card.
Use the double it sits beside.
Type the total and check it.
play.kidTip: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
play.audioPrompt: Near doubles! This fact is one more than a double you know.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. It is one away from a double you know.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Naming the double first is the strategy. A child who jumps straight to the answer has not used it, even when they are right.

lessons.title: Near Doubles: One Less

play.shortDesc: A Double, and One Less
play.targetObjective: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
stepByStep: Read the fact on the card.
Use the double it sits beside.
Type the total and check it.
play.kidTip: A near double is one step from a double you already know.
play.audioPrompt: Near doubles! This fact is one less than a double you know.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. It is one away from a double you know.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Going down from a double is harder than going up, and worth its own lesson: the same relationship, the other direction.

lessons.title: Make Five

play.shortDesc: Say how many more counters a five-frame needs
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
stepByStep: Some counters are already in the frame.
Tap empty spaces until the frame is full.
The answer is how many you had to add — not the whole frame.
play.kidTip: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
play.audioPrompt: Make five! How many more counters does the frame need?

prompts.default: You have {a}. How many more to make {size}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The answer is the part added, not the total. A child who says five has read the frame rather than the question.

lessons.title: Make Ten

play.shortDesc: Say how many more counters a ten-frame needs
play.targetObjective: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
stepByStep: Some counters are already in the frame.
Tap empty spaces until both rows are full.
The answer is how many you had to add.
play.kidTip: Fill the frame right up. Count only the ones you put in.
play.audioPrompt: Make ten! How many more counters does the frame need?

prompts.default: You have {a}. How many more to make {size}?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Friends of ten are the facts every bridging strategy stands on. Known instantly, they turn 8 + 5 into 10 + 3.

lessons.title: Reach the Next Ten

play.shortDesc: Choose the jump that lands exactly on the next ten
play.targetObjective: Jump to the round number, not past it.
stepByStep: Find the two tens your number sits between.
Work out how far it is to the one above.
Choose that jump — landing past it does not count.
play.kidTip: Jump to the round number, not past it.
play.audioPrompt: Reach the next ten! Which jump lands exactly on the round number?

prompts.default: Which jump takes {a} to the next ten?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Reaching the round number is the move inside every make-ten strategy. Practised alone, it stops being the hard part of 47 + 8.

lessons.title: Reach the Next Hundred

play.shortDesc: Choose the jump that lands exactly on the next hundred
play.targetObjective: Jump to the round hundred, not past it.
stepByStep: Find the two hundreds your number sits between.
Work out how far it is to the one above.
Choose that jump.
play.kidTip: Jump to the round hundred, not past it.
play.audioPrompt: Reach the next hundred! Which jump lands exactly on the round number?

prompts.default: Which jump takes {a} to the next hundred?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same move one place up. A child who sees it as the same move has generalised; one who meets it as a new fact has not.

lessons.title: Break One Number Apart
lessons.concept: Splitting an Addend to Reach Ten

play.shortDesc: Split the second number so the first can reach ten
play.targetObjective: Give the first number just enough to reach ten, then add what is left.
stepByStep: Work out what the first number needs to reach ten.
Take that much out of the second number.
Whatever is left over is the other part.
play.kidTip: Give the first number just enough to reach ten, then add what is left.
play.audioPrompt: Break a number apart! Give the first one just enough to reach ten.

prompts.default: Break {b} apart so {a} can reach ten.

lessons.pedagogyTip: This is where make-ten becomes a strategy rather than a fact: the child chooses the split, and the split is the thinking.

lessons.title: Split Both Numbers

play.shortDesc: Break each two-digit number into its tens and its ones
play.targetObjective: Every two-digit number is some tens and some ones.
stepByStep: Look at the first number's tens and ones.
Write each part in its box — the tens as a whole ten.
Do the same for the second number.
play.kidTip: Every two-digit number is some tens and some ones.
play.audioPrompt: Split both numbers! Each one is some tens and some ones.

prompts.default: Split each number into its tens and its ones.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Splitting both is what makes adding by place possible. Writing forty rather than four is the part that has to be right.

lessons.title: Use a Fact You Know
lessons.concept: Deriving from a Fact You Hold

play.shortDesc: Pick the nearby fact that helps, then use it
play.targetObjective: Pick a fact you already know that is close to this one.
stepByStep: Look at the fact you have been given.
Choose the nearby fact you already know — a double is usually closest.
Count on or back from it to reach the answer.
play.kidTip: Pick a fact you already know that is close to this one.
play.audioPrompt: Use a fact you know! Which one is closest to this?

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Which fact would help?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Choosing the helper is the lesson. Every option offered is a real fact, so a child cannot pick well by spotting the silly one.

lessons.title: Fact Families

play.shortDesc: Write all four facts that three numbers make together
play.targetObjective: The same three numbers make four different facts.
stepByStep: Look at the three numbers in the family.
Two facts add them together, in either order.
Two facts take one part away from the whole.
play.kidTip: The same three numbers make four different facts.
play.audioPrompt: Fact families! The same three numbers make four different facts.

prompts.default: {a}, {b} and {sum} make a family. Fill in all four.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Seeing addition and subtraction as one family is what later makes a missing addend a question a child can answer.

lessons.title: Switch the Numbers
lessons.concept: Order Does Not Change the Total

play.shortDesc: Say the same fact the other way round
play.targetObjective: You can add in either order and the total does not change.
stepByStep: Read the fact you are given.
Say it the other way round — it starts with the other number.
The total is exactly the same.
play.kidTip: You can add in either order and the total does not change.
play.audioPrompt: Switch the numbers! The same fact the other way round makes the same total.

prompts.default: {a} plus {b}. Which is the same fact the other way round?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Commutativity is what makes starting from the larger number allowed. Stated as its own idea, it stops being a trick.
